title: Solving Quantitative Reasoning Problems with Language Models (Minerva)
one_line: Continuing to train PaLM on 38.5B tokens of arXiv and math web pages, combined with majority-vote sampling, gives Minerva state-of-the-art results on MATH, GSM8k and MMLU-STEM without external tools, with little evidence of memorization.

metaphors.idea: Stacked blocks showing the training recipe: general PaLM pretraining base, topped by math web pages (47.5%) and arXiv (47.5%) technical data, scaling across 8B/62B/540B models

Many sampled solution paths converging on one answer: k=256 chain-of-thought samples grouped by final answer, with the most common one chosen (majority vote), contrasted with pass@k which keeps climbing while majority voting saturates
A worked solution shown as a ruled, step-by-step derivation (question, target, model output), with a rule separating the model's approach from the ground-truth approach to show it is not memorized

notes: Results are dense: Table 3 (MATH, OCWCourses, GSM8k, MMLU-STEM across PaLM/Minerva 8B/62B/540B, with and without maj1@k, plus davinci-002 and published SOTA) is the key table, and Figure 4 gives subtopic bar charts. Highlight the headline gains, e.g. MATH 50.3% (Minerva 540B maj1@k) vs 6.9% previous SOTA, and GSM8k 78.5% vs 74.4%. Show one or two worked LaTeX examples (Fig 1 line equation, Fig 3 disk kinetic energy) with equations rendered cleanly. The error analysis (Table 4: incorrect reasoning 82, incorrect calculation 70 out of 201) and false positive rates (Table 5) merit a short slide each. The memorization section (BLEU overlap, modified problems, scatter plots in Fig 5) is a three-part argument, best shown as a clear three-step structure. Limitations should be stated plainly: no automatic verification, no calculators or tools. Tone is sober and evidence-driven, not hype. Keep text sparse and let tables, charts and equations carry the talk.
